reference.source: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Denotes true softening, fibrillation and degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage, distinct from though overlapping with patellofemoral pain syndrome.
Retropatellar pain is worse on stairs, squatting, kneeling and prolonged sitting, the classic theatre or cinema sign.
The Outerbridge classification grades severity arthroscopically from softening through fissuring to full-thickness cartilage loss with exposed bone.
Crepitus and a positive patellar grind test are common but non-specific findings.
Typically affects younger, often female patients with maltracking, quadriceps imbalance or an increased Q-angle.
Articular cartilage is aneural, so pain arises from the innervated subchondral bone, synovium and peripatellar soft tissues rather than the cartilage lesion itself.
Management is predominantly conservative, centred on activity modification, quadriceps and hip strengthening and patellar taping.
Arthroscopic chondroplasty is reserved for selected refractory cases and does not reverse the underlying process.
reference.pathophysiology: Chondromalacia patellae describes structural degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage that progresses from softening and swelling, through fissuring and fibrillation, to fragmentation and eventual full-thickness loss exposing subchondral bone. It is driven by abnormal patellofemoral contact stress arising from maltracking, lateral patellar tilt or subluxation, muscle imbalance with a weak vastus medialis obliquus and a tight lateral retinaculum, malalignment such as an increased Q-angle or trochlear dysplasia, or direct trauma, all of which concentrate load on focal cartilage areas. Because articular cartilage is avascular and aneural, the lesion is not itself the direct pain generator; symptoms arise from altered load transmission to richly innervated subchondral bone, synovial irritation and peripatellar soft tissues. In some patients it represents an early stage on the continuum towards patellofemoral osteoarthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Patellofemoral pain syndrome without structural cartilage change
Osteochondritis dissecans in adolescents or referred hip and lumbar pain
additionalInvestigations: Skyline/Merchant and lateral radiographs to assess patellar tilt, subluxation, joint space and alignment
MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences such as fat-suppressed proton density to grade chondral change
Clinical assessment of the Q-angle and lower limb rotational alignment
Evaluation of patellar tracking and vastus medialis obliquus function
Assessment of hip abductor and core strength
Arthroscopy for direct Outerbridge grading in refractory or surgical cases
redFlags: Effusion with warmth suggesting inflammatory or septic arthritis
Locking or true giving way suggesting a chondral flap or loose body
Progressive rest or night pain or systemic symptoms suggesting neoplasm or infection
Rapidly progressive joint space loss indicating established osteoarthritis
reference.prognosis: Symptoms frequently improve with sustained conservative rehabilitation, but established high-grade cartilage lesions may persist and can progress to patellofemoral osteoarthritis; surgical outcomes are variable.
pitfalls: Using the term interchangeably with patellofemoral pain syndrome and overcalling structural disease.
Over-relying on imaging when chondral findings correlate poorly with symptoms.
Neglecting proximal hip and core contributions to patellar maltracking.
Proceeding to early surgery such as lateral release or chondroplasty before exhausting rehabilitation.
Missing an underlying instability or malalignment that is driving the cartilage wear.
references: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: The mainstay is a sustained physiotherapy programme strengthening the quadriceps, especially vastus medialis obliquus, together with hip abductor and core conditioning
Modify activity and manage load to reduce provocative patellofemoral stress from stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting
Use simple analgesia or a short course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for symptomatic relief
Correct biomechanics with patellar taping or bracing and foot orthoses where malalignment contributes
Address contributory factors such as a tight lateral retinaculum and an increased Q-angle, and support weight management
Reserve surgery, such as arthroscopic chondroplasty, lateral release or realignment by tibial tubercle transfer, for refractory cases
